item.title: INSTRUCTION: 10 ways to get a deal on a cruise
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Getting a great deal on a cruise is getting harder. Strong demand for cruises allows cruise lines to raise fares significantly and cut back on last-minute discounts to fill unsold cabins. As a result, the fares you’ll find for cruises can sometimes be much higher — by 20% or more — than what you were expecting. So, how do you get the best cruise deal if you’re trying to book a cruise for this year and beyond? To start: Don’t panic. Even if fares seem high, you can find ways to save when booking a vacation at sea. Below, we’ve assembled 10 of our top tips for finding a bargain on a cruise. These are travel hacks that can work any time — not just when fares are rising. Combine a few of these strategies, and you are sure to find the best cruise deals available on your next sailing. As is the case for resorts on land, floating resorts (i.e., cruise ships) can be significantly less expensive during the “offseason” travel months of September, October and November. These are months when kids are typically back in school and family travel drops off, resulting in diminished demand for many types of travel, including cruises. These months also fall during the Caribbean's hurricane season, which keeps some people away from land resorts and cruise ships in the region. In addition to the fall months, the offseason period for cruising generally includes parts of January and February, but it varies by region. Traditionally, the summer months of June, July and August have been high season in many cruise destinations like the Caribbean, Europe and Alaska. The periods around major holidays — such as Easter, Thanksgiving, Christmas and New Year’s Day — also are considered the busy season for cruising and bring higher prices. It’s a growing truism of the cruise world: The earlier you book, the better price you’ll get. Cruise lines often open departures for bookings with the lowest prices at which they want to sell the trips. Then, as the departures start filling up, they slowly raise prices on the remaining inventory. To get the best price on any particular sailing, your best bet, in many cases, is to book right when the sailing opens for sale. This means planning way in advance. Many cruise lines open their reservations for sailings two or even three years before departure. Booking far in advance can pay off in more ways than one. One big advantage to booking ahead of time is that you’re far more likely to get the exact cabin type you want. On many ships, the least expensive cabins and most expensive suites often sell out first and quickly. Worried you might miss out on a deal by booking a cruise super far in advance? Here’s the good news: If, for some reason, the cost of your cruise drops at a later date, you often can get your fare reduced to match the lower price (see, Monitor Your Fare, below). As noted above, cruise lines typically offer their lowest fare for any given sailing just after it opens for booking — often two or even three years before it’s scheduled to begin. Generally, the fare will only go up as the sailing date approaches, but, in some cases, cruise lines will drop the price of a cruise significantly at the last minute. This can happen when the line finds itself with a lot of unsold cabins for a voyage. If you’re flexible and can travel on short notice, you can sometimes find a last-minute deal for a cruise where the line is scrambling to fill berths just before a departure. A key thing to know here is that last-minute discounting isn’t as common as it used to be. Like airlines, cruise lines have become much more savvy about revenue management over the years, and it’s rarer that they find themselves with a lot of unsold inventory on sailings just before departure. You’ll also have to be flexible to take advantage of these deals. If you have a specific cabin type on a specific sailing on a specific ship that you’re eyeing for a vacation, you can’t count on it being available — especially not at a rock-bottom rate. Also, don’t forget that you may pay a lot more for flights to a cruise and a precruise hotel if you wait until the last minute to book them. Last-minute cruise deals often work best for travelers who live near a departure port that they can reach easily by car, avoiding the cost of last-minute flights and hotels. Booking early doesn't mean you've locked in the lowest fare. Cruise lines use dynamic pricing. Fares can rise or fall even after you book, so it pays to keep an eye on prices. If the fare drops for the same sailing and cabin category, you may be able to get the lower price. This is often the case until the last few months before the sailing begins, when the cruise enters what’s known as the final payment window. At that point, the fare you’ve paid is locked in. Cruise lines won't necessarily adjust your booking automatically — you'll need to ask. Policies vary by line. Many of the big lines — including Royal Caribbean, Carnival, Norwegian and Princess — have some form of price-protection or “best price guarantee” program. Most times, you can reprice your booking at the lower fare before making your final payment. After final payment, your options narrow. Some lines will offer an upgrade, onboard credit or a future cruise credit equal to the difference, rather than cash. To request a price adjustment, contact the cruise line or your travel agent with your booking number and details of the lower fare. Make sure you're comparing the same sailing and cabin category, and note that not all fare types allow for changes to the fare you’ve paid after booking. Read the fine print, too. Repricing can mean giving up promotions tied to your original booking, such as onboard credit — and some lines exclude shorter sailings. Some cruise-specialist travel agents will monitor your fare for you. You can also set up fare alerts that will send you an email if the price has dropped. At many big lines, you’ll find that the newest, most amenity-filled cruise ships sell at a premium price. Older ships come with a discount. The older ships are, of course, older, and they sometimes don’t have quite as much to offer on board as the newer ships. But if you’re looking for a deal, they can bring great value. If you're not fussy about where you sleep, there's another way to trim your fare. That's booking a guarantee cabin. A guarantee fare lets you choose the category — inside, oceanview, balcony or suite — but not the specific cabin. The line assigns your room later, sometimes just days before sailing. What you're guaranteed is a cabin in the category you paid for, or a better one. In return for that flexibility, lines often price guarantee cabins below the cheapest cabin you can pick yourself in the same category. The savings vary by line, sailing and category, but can run from roughly $50 to $200 or more per person. That's the trade-off: You give up control over deck and location. You could land near the elevators or a noisy venue. If you need a specific spot — close to the dining room for mobility reasons, adjoining cabins for a family or midship if you're prone to seasickness — book a cabin you choose yourself. Occasionally, when a ship is full in your category, a guarantee passenger sometimes gets bumped up to a better one. This is the exception, rather than the rule. Plenty of guarantee bookings end up in the least desirable cabin in the category. Are you a plan-it-yourself type of traveler? We get it. Many of TPG’s staffers are that way, too. But even if you book all your land trips on your own, you might want to use a travel agent who is a cruise specialist to book your next voyage. One big reason is that cruise-selling travel agents often have access to lower bulk fares for sailings that aren’t available to the general public. Big travel agencies will block out large chunks of cabins on ships soon after they open for booking to lock in such group fares, then sell them over the coming months. When you book through cruise travel agents, you can sometimes receive lower fares and extra perks like onboard credit or amenities. Travel agents specializing in cruising will also be able to guide you through the many types of cabin categories on some cruise ships and steer you away from cabins to avoid. Plus, they’ll be there for you when things go wrong on a cruise. You don't have to be planning an extended family reunion or large event to get a group deal. Most cruise lines treat a booking of several cabins as a group — and they reward it. The threshold varies by line; eight cabins is common, though some lines start lower. Perks can include a discounted group fare, onboard credit and, for the person who organizes the booking, a free berth. That's essentially one free fare, not including taxes and fees. The bigger the group, the bigger the perks. Even if you aren't traveling with a crowd, it's possible to build one. Cruise forums and social media groups often organize sailing-specific meetups where strangers pool cabins under a single group booking to reach the threshold. Each cabin typically pays its own fare, and some organizers pass part of the savings along to the group. Group bookings can come with their own payment schedules and change or cancellation rules, so read the terms before you commit. These bookings usually run through a cruise-specialist travel agent or the line's group desk. Some of the best bargains in the cruise world are the voyages that cruise ships make as they reposition from one part of the world to another. This is because cruise lines often have trouble selling these trips. They typically have oddball itineraries with very few port calls and lots of sea days — something that doesn’t appeal to many cruisers. Repositioning cruises also tend to be considerably longer than standard weekend getaways or weeklong voyages — a turnoff to the many travelers who have limited vacation days. To sell them, cruise lines often have to reduce their per-day prices sharply, making them a bargain. Among the most common repositioning cruises are sailings between the Caribbean and Europe in the spring as lines move ships to Europe for the summer. Similarly, there’s a wave of repositioning cruises between Europe and the Caribbean in the fall. You’ll also find some repositioning cruises every year between the Caribbean and Alaska and between the West Coast and Asia or Australia. Some cruise lines offer reduced fares or special perks to special groups, these include military members and veterans, teachers, seniors and residents of particular states or regions. Terms vary widely. Eligibility for spouses, age cutoffs and whether the discount can be combined with other promotions all differ by line, so ask when you book and have your documentation ready. item.title: At Our Annual Points of View Summit, Experts Make Their 2027 Travel Predictions
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
When planning our 2026 Points of View Summit, we wanted to be sure to set time aside to hear directly from our travel specialists—the behind-the-scenes experts who work tirelessly work to curate ambitious and deeply personal itineraries around the world. Spliced between compelling panels on Lowcountry heritage, summer travel trends, and the evolving appeal of all-inclusive stays, the breakouts allowed for extended discussions with Traveler editors on a range of themes. From culinary experiences inspired by Hilton Head Island's Gullah cuisine, to the evolving dynamics of multigenerational travel and a new guard of ultra-luxe globetrotters, we got the inside scoop on where travelers are going and how they're getting there. What's new in the world of culinary travel? Inspired by Hilton Head Island's rich tapestry of culinary traditions, senior features editor Megan Spurrell and editorial assistant Skyli Alvarez led a discussion on traveling for taste—from the rising interest in foraging over traditional cooking classes to the draw of big-name chefs contrasted with harder-to-find local gems, and the hotspots that deserve to be on our food maps. Our specialists all agreed that travelers yearn for “authentic” food moments, though defining authenticity—and actually finding it—often becomes tricky. To Omolola Campbell, sixth-gen Gullah descendant and executive producer of Gullah short documentary The Spirit We Move With, it's about who provides the experience. “Taking a cooking class is much different than getting it from a local chef who can tell stories about why a dish means so much to this locality,” she said, explaining how so many of South Carolina's Gullah dishes contain okra because its seeds were sown into the hair of West Africans who were brought to the South for slavery. The plant has come to represent resilience, and it's that integral context, according to her, that gives a meal its soul. “That's how you differentiate the person who really knows why they're cooking what they're cooking,” Campbell concluded. What does multigenerational travel look today? When it comes to multigenerational trips, the grandchildren are choosing the destinations and the grandparents are paying—it's their way of leaving a legacy amongst those dearest to them. During a discussion led by global executive director of video Dana Kravis and commerce director Madison Flager, our travel specialists observed that, because people today tend to wait longer to have children, grandparents are older than they used to be. Travelers in their 80s and 90s are increasingly joining trips, shifting the multigenerational travel dynamic away from the traditional picture of grandparents in their 70s. To trip designers, this means there must be layers of options catering to different activity and exertion levels. Many in this session agreed the most successful family trips provide opportunities for separating and coming back together. Three itinerary choices in one day are ideal, so younger folks can be out and about, with the whole family reuniting for mealtimes and perhaps an afternoon activity. Boat and yacht experiences were especially recommended as spaces where the family is forced to be together—grandkids cannot simply run off and do their own thing. What's luxury to one traveler might seem the furthest from it to another; some long for jam-packed, once-in-a-lifetime itineraries, while others want total disconnection and the privilege to do absolutely nothing for a week. Features director Rebecca Misner and commerce writer Jessica Sulima led this breakout, as specialists debated the definition of luxury itself. “Luxury is being able to pass on meaning to kids [and] exposing families to the broader world and its cultures,” Virgi Schiffino Kennedy, managing partner at Lux Voyage, said of its intangible appeal. To Ruchi Harnal, founder of Harnal Travel, true luxury “is not about the resort or the villa but the personalization of the trip.” As for who’s spending money on trips? Thomas Robinson, MR at Dehouche, has observed that Gen Z and Millennials are more inclined to spend but want to know where that money goes. Additionally, the specialists largely agreed they’re seeing a shift away from parents taking their children on trips, and towards 30- and 40-somethings treating their parents to a vacation. In Harnal's experience, milestone birthdays and anniversaries are driving clients to book a trip. What is the impact of overtourism, price inflation, and rising temperatures on our Euro summers? Director of special projects Lale Arikoglu and commerce editor Meaghan Kenny opened the floor for our specialists. “If you’re thinking of traveling to the Dolomites, consider Switzerland instead. There’s history and beautiful scenery with fewer crowds,” Brian Dore, owner of CIU Travel, said. For the hiking curious, some added that Switzerland offers plenty of one-day hiking trails or “soft adventure” travel—three-to-four days combined with a lake or city destination. Others agreed that traveling to the Alps offers a significant advantage—higher elevations means cooler temperatures—and that Slovenia is a great alternative to Italy. To dodge the crowds, travelers might also consider Belgium, Denmark, or Norway (where ocean ships and river cruises are opening earlier in March). For families, consider Umbria (hot tip: plenty of festival and craft opportunities for kids), Austria, Ireland, or Croatia. For those who want to stick with more tried-and-tested European itineraries next summer, consider going as early as possible, for instance, in May instead of August. When it comes to traveling to France specifically, folks advised flying into Paris or Nice, then venturing out to the countryside or oft-overlooked Atlantic Coast. And our specialists could not stress it enough: Always, always check the temperatures in advance of your trip. As discussed by Mei Zhang, chairman and founder at WildChina, during the panel on summer travel, the demand for travel to Asia is only increasing. Global features director Erin Florio and editorial assistant Kat Chen continued the conversation with travel specialists on the destinations and experiences driving this growth. For Silk Road Treasure Tours president Zulya Rajabova and her clients, it's the destinations with indispensable craft identities, such as Samarkand in Uzbekistan with its millennia-old design traditions, that make the continent so varied yet distinct. Meanwhile, Marigold Wood, travel designer at Blonde Atlas, explained that she's been recommending routes going through China, such as Yunnan's tea trails, which offer trekking and hiking opportunities. For Ethan Crowley, lead trip designer at Asia Desk Ltd, educating his travelers on navigating countries like Cambodia, beyond their most-visited landmarks, is key. If 2026 was the year of the fan, 2027 is ushering in even more reasons to travel for entertainment. Associate editor Charlie Hobbs and commerce writer Jessica Chapel helmed this breakout on the sporting events, music festivals, and art fairs that specialists are seeing people travel for (and the subsequent hurdles they must overcome to). From Pink at the Sphere, where access requires a Venetian hotel package to the Ryder Cup at Adare Manor, where full-house and package buyouts, high-demand events are increasingly forcing bundled purchases. The specialists also highlighted how limited legal protections in the States enables extreme ticket scalping for stadium concerts and makes domestic events increasingly unaffordable. Stephanie Malakie, founder of Empress Travel Club pointed to a related challenge: With so many events and providers, travel advisors find it hard to filter the options and identify the right fit for clients. Rather than just acquiring a ticket, specialists agreed the focus should be on curating the surrounding experience or tapping into evergreen and niche experiential travel, with events like the Jets playing in London or F1 in Shanghai. Cultural milestones like Vatican City trips featuring Papal Blessings or European Christmas markets pair well with entertainment, too. To Zhang, set-jetting to filming locations also offers value, minus the headache of peak-event ticketing. Everyone is hiking, or so it seems. Helmed by Jamie Spain, travel bookings commerce editor, and Hannah Towey, news editor, this breakout explored nature as wellness and why it is we're increasingly longing for all things outdoorsy. However, our specialists offered a frank reality check on our dumbphone fantasies. “Guests all want to have access [to Wi-Fi] for emergency reasons at a minimum… I don’t have a single guest who wants to [fully] digital detox," Kate Doty, trip designer at Geographic Expeditions, said. It seems that many travelers want to be disconnected until the time comes for true disconnection, and Lou Lagrange, trip consultant at Luxury Travel Advisor, added, “Even planning for national park trips, [you have to] warn them there won’t be Wi-Fi.” However, the group observed that services such as having photographers on small ships, helps reduce a traveler's dependency on their phones. There's still a real demand for glamping, as guests want access to nature but with a side of luxury. And when it comes to extreme weather events, instead of having travelers write off entire regions or countries, Doty has figured out collaborative ways to shelve them for potential future trips. In Travel Studio founder Kerri Lisa's case, it's a matter of reframing the perks of a destination and its seasons; the rainy season, for example, might be exceptionally lush and green. There's always something to be learned in welcoming a bit of playful unpredictability into our itineraries.

item.title: INSTRUCTION: 31 Cranberry Recipes for Thanksgiving and Beyond
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Cranberries are doing a lot more than keeping turkey company. Fresh berries bring a sharp, lip-puckering bite to pies, cakes, and relishes. Dried cranberries deliver little bursts of sweetness to rice dishes and cookies. Even the canned stuff has its moments (see: sweet-and-sour chicken). Cranberries are particularly good at turning themselves into sauce, thanks to their generous supply of natural pectin. But there’s much more to make with them: a towering cranberry meringue pie, chewy pinwheel cookies striped with red wine jam, tangy dressings for bitter greens, and plenty of festive drinks. The recipes below make a case for stocking up on fresh cranberries when they’re in season—roughly October through December—and keeping a bag or two in the freezer for the rest of the year. Look for firm, glossy cranberries and discard any that are soft, shriveled, or bruised. A few pale pink berries are nothing to worry about. Keep unwashed cranberries in their original bag in the refrigerator for up to four weeks, though they’re best used sooner. To stock up, freeze them in their original packaging or spread clean, thoroughly dried berries on a baking sheet until frozen, then transfer to a freezer bag. They’ll keep their quality for up to a year. Many cooked cranberry recipes work with frozen berries straight from the freezer; check the recipe before thawing. Have part of a bag left over? These ideas from the BA archives put even a small quantity to good use. - Make sugared cranberries. Soak whole, pricked cranberries overnight in simple syrup, then drain, roll in superfine sugar, and let dry. They’re especially pretty on cakes and cocktails. - Roast them with herbs. Toss fresh cranberries with olive oil, a little sugar, and chopped thyme. Roast at 400°F until softened, about 15–20 minutes, then serve with chicken or pork. - Turn them into salsa. Pulse fresh cranberries with brown sugar, shallot, jalapeño, lime zest, and lime juice. Let the mixture stand for about 15 minutes, then finish with cilantro. Spoon it over roast meats or goat cheese crostini. - Make cranberry butter. Cook fresh cranberries with a little maple syrup until thick and jammy. Cool completely, then beat into softened butter for a bright pink spread for toast, muffins, and biscuits. - Use them in breakfast. Stir a handful of fresh cranberries into simmering oatmeal with apples and other berries, or fold them into a quick bread or muffin batter for pockets of tart fruit.

item.title: American Airlines announces updates to its Phoenix Admirals Clubs
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
The airport lounge wars aren't heating up only among premium credit card issuers. Airlines are stepping up their own lounge investments, too. American Airlines has been on a tear of its own lately, including upgrades and a huge new Admirals Club at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) Terminal C, a massive (and much-needed) new lounge complex at its Charlotte Douglas International Airport (CLT) hub and the reopening of its Flagship Dining offering at Los Angeles International Airport (LAX). Now, Phoenix Sky Harbor International Airport (PHX) is the airline's next base scheduled for a glow-up. All three Phoenix Admirals Clubs are getting refreshed American Airlines currently fields three Admirals Clubs at PHX — two in Concourse A and one in Concourse B at Terminal 4 — all of which are being updated. Admirals Club Concourse A between gates A19 and A21 The first lounge where flyers will see changes is this diminutive lounge in Concourse A. Effective immediately, there will be a new food service area and expanded food and beverage offerings. More importantly, though, the airline plans to nearly triple the combined lounge footprint of its Concourse A lounges, which include another Admirals Club near gates A7 and A9; it will increase seating capacity by around 150%, and add new furniture and finishes. Hopefully those will reflect the more sophisticated aesthetics American Airlines has been pivoting toward, starting with its Ronald Reagan National Airport (DCA) outpost. Admirals Club Concourse B between gates B5 and B7 Over in Concourse B, one of the airline's other Admirals Clubs will see a new self-service food and beverage area (aka a buffet and bar), a 20% increase in seating capacity and new interiors. “Phoenix continues to be an important hub in our network, and these investments reflect our commitment to giving customers more space, comfort and convenience when they travel through PHX,” American’s chief customer officer Heather Garboden said in an online statement. “While we look forward to the development of the new West Terminal, these enhancements will help create an even more seamless travel experience for the millions of customers who pass through Phoenix each year.” The updates make sense and are badly needed at an American Airlines hub where the Admirals Clubs frequently become overcrowded. The airline carries over 20 million passengers through PHX each year and operates over 300 peak daily departures, so expanding and refreshing its lounges there is a priority to continue attracting premium passengers. Though details are still scant, American Airlines is updating its three Admirals Clubs at PHX. Passengers should see immediate changes at its Concourse A club near gates A19 and A21, but travelers will have to wait for the larger changes, which will include an expanded footprint and updated interiors. It remains to be seen what other amenities might be available. Related reading:

item.title: INSTRUCTION: How to Blind-Bake Pie Crust—and When You Need To
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
The road to pie perfection is paved in pitfalls. I’ve fallen into plenty of them throughout my baking career. The infamous “soggy bottom” is among the most common, but it’s easy to avoid. Blind baking—baking the crust before adding the filling—helps prevent an underbaked crust by giving the pastry a head start in the oven or cooking it completely before the filling goes in. But getting the crust to the right color depends on what you’re planning to fill it with. A pale, partially baked shell might be perfect for one pie, while another needs a deep golden brown crust before you add even a spoonful of filling. Here’s how to know when enough color is enough. When should you blind-bake pie crust? Blind baking is especially useful when the filling needs less time in the oven than the crust does. For custard pies, like pumpkin pie, partially baking the shell gives the pastry a head start so it doesn’t end up uncooked beneath a set filling. For pies with no-bake fillings, such as chocolate pudding pie or cranberry curd pie, the crust needs to be fully baked before it’s filled. Most traditional fruit pies don’t need blind baking. Their fillings and crusts spend enough time in the oven together for the pastry to cook through. There are exceptions, particularly single-crust fruit pies topped with a crumble. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, starts with a thoroughly blind-baked shell before the filling goes in. Follow your recipe’s instructions rather than assuming every fruit pie needs the same treatment. Start with a good pie dough. Roll it out, fit it into the pie plate, and crimp the edge. Chill the shaped shell for at least 15 minutes before baking; cold dough holds its shape better in the oven, reducing the risk of shrinking or slumping. Next, line the shell with parchment paper and fill it with pie weights. Crumpling the parchment first, then unfolding it, helps it conform to the shell. The weights hold the dough against the pan while it bakes, preventing the bottom from puffing up and the sides from collapsing. You can buy ceramic pie weights or use dried beans, rice, or stainless-steel ball bearings. I’m partial to the ball bearings: They’re small enough to settle into the corners of the pie plate and heavy enough to hold the dough firmly in place. Not everyone in the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen agrees. Editors Jesse Szewczyk and Rebecca Firkser prefer lighter alternatives. In their experience, heavy metal weights can compress the dough, limiting the expansion of the buttery layers that make pie crust flaky. Jesse uses dried beans or rice; Rebecca prefers dried chickpeas or even granulated sugar, a technique popularized by baking expert Stella Parks. All of these options can work. Whichever you choose, fill the parchment-lined shell generously, supporting the sides all the way to the rim. Leave the weights in place until the crust looks dry and set and the parchment releases easily; removing them too soon can cause the sides to slump. This method uses our Perfect Pie Crust dough and makes one 9"-diameter pie shell. It produces an evenly golden crust; if your pie calls for a paler or more deeply browned shell, follow its specific baking instructions and use the visual guide below. - 1 disk Perfect Pie Crust dough, chilled - Special Equipment: pie weights, dried beans, or rice - Remove 1 disk Perfect Pie Crust dough from the refrigerator and let sit at room temperature about 5 minutes, until just pliable. Roll out on a lightly floured surface to a 12" round, about ⅛" thick. Brush off excess flour and transfer to a 9"-diameter pie plate, preferably metal. Gently ease the dough into the bottom and sides without stretching it. Trim, leaving about 1" overhang. Fold the overhang onto itself, pressing to seal, and crimp as desired. Chill 15 minutes. - Place a rack in the lower third of the oven; preheat to 375°F. Set the pie plate on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet. Crumple 2 sheets of parchment paper, then unfold them so they'll fit more easily against the crust. Line the crust with the parchment and fill to the edges with pie weights, dried beans, or rice. - Bake until the edges are golden brown and the bottom looks set and opaque when you carefully lift the parchment to check, about 30–35 minutes. Remove from the oven and reduce the oven temperature to 325°F. Carefully lift out the parchment and weights. - Return the crust to the oven and bake until the bottom and sides are evenly golden brown all over, 12–18 minutes more. If you’re using the shell for a pie that requires further baking, follow that recipe’s instructions for the appropriate doneness. For a no-bake filling, make sure the shell is fully baked before filling. Some pie recipes call for docking (pricking the bottom and sides of the dough with a fork) before baking. This allows steam to escape and helps prevent uneven puffing, but doesn’t replace the support of pie weights. Follow your recipe’s instructions; docking isn’t necessary for every blind-baked crust. Do Ahead: A fully blind-baked crust can be made up to 2 days ahead. Let cool completely, wrap well, and store at room temperature until ready to fill. How long should you blind-bake pie crust? The short answer: It depends on what you’re putting inside. Some pies need only a partially baked crust, while others call for a shell that’s deeply golden brown. Oven temperatures vary, different pie plates conduct heat differently, and the filling determines how much additional baking the crust will get. Use the recipe’s timing as a guide, but watch the color and texture of the pastry. Here’s what to look for. Fruit pies need a pale base because they bake a looong time. Or at least, that’s often the thinking. If you’re making a single-crust variety topped with a crumble, such as our Blueberry Crumble Pie, and the recipe calls for blind-baking, you might want to start with an anemic crust. It’ll have plenty of time to brown as the juices thicken. A pale, partially baked crust should look set rather than raw. The bottom should look set and opaque with some light golden patches, while the crimped edge may already be noticeably browned. The crust will continue to develop color once the filling goes in. Don’t assume fruit pies always need a pale shell. Our Peach-Blueberry Pie, for example, calls for a well-browned crust before the fruit and crumble go in. And many double-crust fruit pies don’t need blind baking at all. A lightly baked shell can also be appropriate for custards that have a substantial bake ahead. BA’s Best Pumpkin Pie starts with a partially baked crust before the custard goes in for at least another hour. The goal is to give the crust enough of a head start without taking it so far that the edges burn before the filling finishes cooking. Custard pies, such as chess and our Lemon Buttermilk Pie, often have shorter bake times than fruit pies, so the crust needs a solid golden base layer to develop enough color by the time the filling sets. Here, you’re looking for more than a crust that’s simply dry and set. The bottom should be evenly golden with no pale, translucent patches, and the sides should have taken on some color too. The rim will generally be a little darker than the bottom, but the whole shell should look well on its way to being fully baked. Our Perfect Pie Crust recipe produces this kind of shell. It calls for baking the weighted crust until the edges are golden, then removing the weights and continuing until the bottom and sides are evenly browned. And some pies need an even more substantial head start. Our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie takes the crust to a dry golden finish before adding a filling that bakes for another 45–55 minutes. The point isn’t that every custard pie needs the same color. It’s that the crust should be baked far enough that it won’t be left pale and doughy by the time the filling is done. Bake the crust to a dark golden brown if you’re adding a no-bake filling, like a pudding or curd. You’re going for a toasty, burnished color, so don’t be gun-shy. Because the filling won’t return to the oven, this is the crust’s one chance to bake all the way through. You want deep color across the entire bottom and up the sides—not just a dark rim surrounding a pale center. The pastry should look dry, crisp, and well browned, without any doughy or translucent spots. After removing the pie weights, continue baking until the shell is fully browned, checking frequently toward the end. Depending on the dough and oven temperature, that might take another 15–20 minutes or longer. Don’t pull it simply because the timer has gone off. Our Cranberry Meringue Pie uses this approach: The crust is baked until golden and dry before the cranberry curd filling goes in. A fully baked shell develops a richer, toastier flavor and is better equipped to stand up to a moist filling. Should you egg-wash a blind-baked crust? Some recipes, including our pumpkin pie, call for brushing a thin layer of beaten egg onto the partially baked shell and returning it to the oven briefly to set. This, ostensibly, creates a barrier between the pastry and the filling, but not all bakers believe the hype. While it can be a useful extra precaution, it is by no means a universal requirement. If your recipe doesn’t call for it, there’s no need to add another step. They’ll be here whenever you need them. Editor’s note: This story was originally published in May 2016 and has been updated with additional reporting and expanded instructions by Phoebe Fry.

item.title: SALES: Best things to do in London at Christmas 2026: the complete guide to festive fun
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
The sheer number of things to do in London at Christmas draws in hundreds of thousands of visitors each year – and tempts residents out to pastures unexplored in search of festive fun. Typically, chilled-out shopping streets and squares across the city transform into sprawling Christmas markets scented by roasted chestnuts and mulled wine, where vendors rustle up other sweet treats and crafty souls sell their wares. Some big-hitters – see Camden Market, Winter Wonderland and the South Bank – are bucket list London attractions for good reason. Big events – such as the unveiling of the Christmas window displays at Harrods and Selfridges – are annual fixtures in the city, while new openings and one-off events bring something different to the festive calendar each year. I might be biased, but there is nowhere as sparkling, fun and cosy as London at Christmas. The city has plenty to offer year-round, but there is something uniquely magical about it when the holidays approach. The shopping streets are illuminated by Christmas lights, the theatres and cinemas add to the festive spirit with seasonal shows and events, Hyde Park gets taken over by Winter Wonderland and the best luxury hotels in London bring out the most elegant decorations. Although the British countryside is equally marvellous this time of year, there is nowhere I’d rather be. Still, you’ll benefit from visiting off-peak once Yuletide mania truly hits the city. Otherwise, there are plenty of Christmas events in London’s leafier suburbs, from wholesome markets to ceramic workshops. For me, a perfect holiday weekend would start with a crisp morning walk in one of the most beautiful London cemeteries, Nunhead Cemetery, with a steaming hot coffee and a cookie from Nūs Nūs, before heading to central London for a shopping spree, a cosy pub lunch in one of the many wonderful pubs in the city, and ending the evening with a fabulous Christmas show – the English National Ballet's Nutcracker being at the top of my list this year. Here, we list the events and attractions the editors at Condé Nast Traveller have their eye on. What is Christmas in London like? Christmas in London is one of the busiest times of the year for all the right reasons. Shopfronts dazzle with spectacular window displays, glittering lights illuminate iconic streets, and the capital's restaurants, bars, hotels, and entertainment venues host a diverse range of shows and events. If you're visiting from out of town, planning your itinerary is essential. Everything from theatre shows to restaurant tables and afternoon teas book up far in advance, especially the glitzy bucket-list spots, so arriving with a list of priorities and travel plans is the key to experiencing the best of the city's festivities. Where to stay in London for Christmas? Where to stay in London at Christmas all depends on what you’ve packed into your itinerary. To be in the tourist heart of the capital, near events and attractions such as the bright lights of Covent Garden and South Bank’s market, you can’t beat a stay at The Savoy, one of the city’s most historic properties. For easy access to the chic pop-ups that take over Mayfair, check into The Lanesborough or Mandarin Oriental Hyde Park, London. For more inspiration, see our complete guide to London’s best Christmas stays. Are the tubes running on Christmas Day? There are usually no Tube, bus or London Overground services on Christmas Day, although taxis, private hire vehicles and some alternative transport options remain available. Services are also reduced over the Christmas period, with additional closures and engineering works possible. TfL has yet to announce its full Christmas 2026 timetable, so travellers should check the official TfL website closer to the date for the latest information. Do pubs open during Christmas? Many London pubs open on Christmas Day, although many only welcome punters for a few hours. While some only open in the afternoon for those craving a festive pint, others go the whole hog, serving multi-course Christmas lunches that require booking well in advance. It's always worth checking opening hours beforehand, particularly with no London Underground services running on Christmas Day. If you can’t get to central London on that day but you still want to cosy up in a pub, this tube-less day is a great opportunity to discover neighbourhood pubs. Skehans is my favourite in southeast London, The Crooked Billet is my go to in Hackney, while The Pig and Butcher cooks up a storm in Islington. Where is the best place to walk in London for Christmas? Everywhere. London is an amazingly walkable city considering its size and, no matter where you are based, you will find a decorated high street or a nice park to stretch your legs. For anyone staying in the heart of the capital, many of London’s green spaces are open as usual on Christmas Day, including Kensington Gardens and Hyde Park – although Winter Wonderland is closed. We’re big fans of building up an appetite on a Christmas morning walk but, if in doubt, head to one of the capital’s commons or heaths, as some gated parks do keep their doors closed. For more inspiration, plot your stroll with our guide to the 23 best walks in London. What is the famous Christmas street in London? Oxford Street and Regent Street are the most famous Christmas streets in London. Carnaby Street is another festive favourite, known for its colourful and creative decorations. However, this is thanks to their dazzling Christmas lights – you won’t find much, if anything, happening across these shopping streets on Christmas Day. However, the lights will continue to illuminate the capital after dark, as will Bond Street’s glittering storefronts. Not all Christmas afternoon teas are made equal. While most hotels offer a version, the ones we recommend at Condé Nast Traveller range from some of the glitziest in town to affordable gems. One of the capital’s most indulgent afternoon teas doubles up as the perfect excuse to smarten up for the afternoon – and peek inside one of the world’s most iconic hotels. It’s The Ritz’s festive afternoon tea, of course. The Palm Court has been transformed into an Edwardian winter wonderland adorned with opulent red and gold trimmings, where cake stands are filled with seasonal treats up until Tuesday 5 January 2027. The hotel's lavish Edwardian interiors are decked out in festive decorations, while guests can tuck into finger sandwiches, Christmas cakes, mince pies and freshly baked scones, accompanied by Christmas carols sung by The Ritz choir. The festive afternoon tea runs from 14 November 2026 to 5 January 2027, with prices starting at £120 per adult. The Rubens at the Palace is marking the season with a Winter Wonderland Afternoon Tea inspired by traditional British Christmas celebrations. Available from 16 November 2026 to 3 January 2027, the experience includes seasonal treats and a glass of mulled wine, with prices starting at £82 per person. Elsewhere, Rosewood London's Festive Art Afternoon Tea at the Mirror Room offers a creative take on the British tradition, while the Chancery Rosewood is serving a festive afternoon tea at Jacqueline, featuring seasonal savouries and intricate pâtisserie by executive pastry chef Marius Dufay. For something slightly more affordable, Hotel Café Royal is offering a festive afternoon tea from 5 November 2026 to 4 January 2027, starting at £85 per person. For more inspiration, see our curated guide to the best Christmas afternoon teas in London. While the likes of Portobello Road and Borough are on everyone’s bucket lists, the large crowds they attract can multiply in the lead-up to Christmas. Winter Wonderland has become a major attraction, taking over Hyde Park between November and December, and is equally busy as families flock from across the country to seek thrills on rollercoaster rides and enjoy immersive experiences such as the Ice Bar. The handful of Christmas markets that pop up across the capital around mid-November (see our guide to the best Christmas markets in London for the ultimate bucket list) can sway in the ‘touristy’ direction. While we’re no strangers to a riverside mulled wine along the Southbank or a mooch and munch under the mistletoe in Borough Market, the most authentic markets tend to be outside the centre of the city. For something a little different, it's worth venturing beyond central London, where independent makers' markets offer a more relaxed alternative to the usual festive crowds. There are several markets celebrating independent makers, bakers and entertainers in London's residential neighbourhoods, just outside the hustle and bustle of the centre. These include Wimbledon Village’s Christmas in the Village celebrations, where face painters, storytellers and arts and crafts experts delight little ones while adults sip boozy hot chocolates and tuck into fare from street food stalls. Another worth visiting is the North London Makers' Market at Abney Hall in Stoke Newington, bringing together independent designers and artists selling everything from handmade ceramics and jewellery to illustrations and homewares. Here are some of our favourite insider Christmas markets to add to the diary throughout December: One of our favourite free things to do at Christmas in London is, quite simply, to set off on foot and soak up the festive atmosphere. London’s iconic department stores and designer flagships put on quite the show this time of year, turning their windows into glittering exhibits that stop shoppers and workers in their tracks. Harrods never fails to put on a dazzling display and, once you’ve gazed through the glass, there’s plenty to explore inside, from its famous Christmas World to festive food and gifts. Over on Oxford Street, Selfridges is another must-see, known for its elaborate Christmas windows, while Fortnum & Mason on Piccadilly traditionally transforms its famous storefront into a festive spectacle. An amble down Bond Street, clutching a steaming hot chocolate, is another way to get in the spirit. Designer brands including Cartier, Dior and Louis Vuitton are known for transforming their storefronts into extravagant festive façades, often outdoing one another year after year. Insider tip: Aside from the designer flagships and department stores, some of London’s most charming delis receive a festive transformation, too. The halls are well and truly decked across Ottolenghi’s London stores, while the shelves at Mayfair’s Farm Shop are overflowing with seasonal treats. See our guide to London’s best festive delis and embark on what might just be the tastiest self-guided city tour going. December is the peak time of the year for the best restaurants in London. Our favourite eateries across the city deck the halls, transforming a great meal into one of the best things to do in London at Christmas. Personally, I have a slight obsession with Noble Rot on Lamb's Conduit Street, so any excuse to sneak in a lunch is welcome – and Christmas makes for a particularly good one. We asked Condé Nast Traveller's resident foodies what their favourite hideouts are for a cosy feast in the lead-up to Christmas: “I love Dean Street Townhouse at Christmas – it's really festive, especially if you bag a seat by the fireplace. Breakfast at The Wolseley is also a festive tradition; we go for a warming breakfast of kedgeree or a full English surrounded by the decorations, and then walk up to Fortnum & Mason to see the windows and grab some Christmas essentials.” Sarah Allard, digital director “In Notting Hill, especially this time of year, I always bounce between Wild (sister restaurant to Wild Tavern in Chelsea Green, which I equally rate) and the Walmer Castle. Both put a big effort into the Christmas cosies, but the Walmer's upstairs dining room is all fireplaces and full-bodied reds.” Tamara Southward, commerce producer “Tucked away down an Islington side street, The Draper’s Arms is the perfect spot to gather with friends and indulge in some festive feasting. The roast here is among the best in London that I’ve found (and trust me when I say, I’ve sampled my fair share). It's served sharer-style in a gorgeous high-ceilinged dining room that feels as though you could be in someone’s, albeit rather lovely, home.” Lucy Bruton, social media manager “For a deliciously classic lunch once Advent rolls around, you can’t beat St John. It’s your favourite chef’s favourite restaurant: order bone marrow on toast, mutton broth and ox heart for a reassuringly Henry VIII spread and let yourself be looked after by a team who never misses a step.” Sarah James, digital editor “The Camberwell Arms is an old faithful for festive meals. It's cosy, comforting and does epic roasts – we typically take over part of the back dining room on one long table, and while away the hours with secret Santa gift giving and cocktail drinking, before ordering big sharing plates to feast on.” Olivia Morelli, digital features editor “Indian food is a must over the festive period, and nowhere does it better than Ganapati in Peckham. The local favourite is a cosy spot that's perfect for sharing – order a bunch of dishes and divide them between friends and family. My pick is always the Tirupati aubergine and Kerala paratha." Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager “The Spread Eagle in Hackney is my favourite festive spot, decorated head-to-toe in tinsel, Friday karaoke to scream Mariah Carey at and an unbeatable vegan roast. It's cosy, and has a great wine list.” Chloe Laws, Acting Senior Manager, Audience Development Meanwhile, it’s fondue season at The Montague on the Gardens. Step into the chalet-style Winter Lodge, complete with a cosy corner fireplace and shimmering Christmas tree for a lip-smacking two-hour experience. The fondue comes with potatoes, pickles, and – most importantly – a hefty amount of bread. The fondue itself is made from Swiss cheeses like Emmental and Vacherin, and tastes incredibly authentic. The friendly, warm service is the cherry (or cheese) on top. For more dining inspiration in London, see our complete guides: Lunch aboard a once-in-a-lifetime luxury train Boarding the British Pullman, a Belmond Train, feels like a once-in-a-lifetime experience whatever the occasion, but come Christmas time, climbing into one of its exquisite vintage carriages is extra special. Guests are greeted at the lounge at Victoria station by a trio of 1920s-inspired performers, The Wild Tonics, who set the tone for a glamorous ride through the English countryside. We settled into Persius, a carriage that dated back to 1938 and that transported the Royal Family to Winston Churchill’s funeral in 1965. Interiors are bedazzled with festive decorations, and Champagne and wine pairings accompany a five-course menu which spans the five-hour journey. Roast dinners don’t come much better than this, but save room for the petite-fours at the end (the mini mince pie felt like my first true taste of Christmas this year). The newest addition to the train is particularly indulgent: Cecilia is designed by Baz Luhrmann and inspired by A Midsummer Night’s Dream. It hosts up to 12 guests and comes with a private lounge and bar, so capacious you barely feel like you’re on a train at all. Sarah Bannerman Dates: From 13th November - 31st December 2026 Location: Train departs and arrives at Victoria Station Come Christmas Eve, the idea of another visit to the main man in red might have lost its appeal, not just for parents but kids, too. Enter Disney on Ice presents Discover the Magic, which sets up residency at the O2 from 24th December to the 3rd January after its annual tour of England. Expect all the current favourite characters to take to the stage, as well as a few classics, from Toy Story’s Woody and Buzz to Princess Belle, Elsa and a mischievous Stitch. Adults will be as wowed as younger guests, as the cast impresses with ice skating, acrobats and a performance that feels so magical you’ll want to visit every year. Sarah Bannerman In general, I think people should enjoy luxury hotels more. There's a certain aura surrounding London's grandest hotels, but the reality is you don't have to spend the night to enjoy the wonderful atmosphere of a grand hotel – sipping a coffee on a plush sofa, surrounded by marble interiors, attentive staff and the sound of a piano, could do wonders for one's mood. This is particularly true at Christmas. Throughout November and December, London's hotels usher in the festive season with spectacular light switch-ons, glitzy parties and, of course, extraordinary Christmas trees, and it would be a real shame not to enjoy the spectacle. Londoners have witnessed the rise of the designer Christmas tree in recent years, with the designer collaborations often making as much of a statement as the trees themselves. Here, we highlight the prettiest Christmas trees in London that are well worth popping into a fabulous hotel lobby to admire – sticking around for Champagne is optional, but a delightful experience. The Ned is bringing back one of London's most spectacular hotel Christmas trees for 2026, taking festive decorations to another level in its magnificent former banking hall. Last year's 6.7-metre-tall tree was created in collaboration with The Macallan, with red velvet bows and copper baubles inspired by the Scottish whisky maker's heritage. While this year's design is still under wraps, visitors can expect plenty of festive cheer, with live music, seasonal dining and Christmas carols performed by Gareth Malone and his choir on selected Sundays in December. If I had to choose my favourite hotel for a Christmas party, it would, without a doubt, be 45 Park Lane. This Dorchester Collection hotel’s festive soiree has become the talk of the town over the years, and for good reason – the food is always delicious, the atmosphere is warm and festive and the entertainment is on point. For Christmas 2026, 45 Park Lane has commissioned British contemporary artist Nicky Hirst to create its annual Artist’s Tree. Titled 'Silent Tinsel', the installation takes inspiration from traditional Victorian Christmas trees, with golden letters and room-key tassel decorations that form playful seasonal anagrams. The tree will be unveiled on 19 November, while the hotel will also offer festive dining at CUT and seasonal cocktails at BAR 45. One of London's most eagerly anticipated Christmas tree unveilings comes courtesy of Claridge's, which has been inviting some of the world's most celebrated designers to reimagine its festive centrepiece since 2009. Last year's spectacular 16-foot tree was designed by Burberry's chief creative officer, Daniel Lee, and adorned with hundreds of bows made from surplus Burberry fabrics, alongside wild foliage, thistles and hand-blown glass baubles. While the designer behind the 2026 installation is yet to be revealed, the hotel's magnificent Mayfair lobby is always worth a visit during the festive season. The London EDITION is another hotel worth visiting during the festive season, particularly for its spectacular lobby and the glamorous Berners Tavern. Last year's Christmas tree was designed in collaboration with cookery writer Skye McAlpine, who transformed it into a whimsical, snow-dusted creation adorned with edible decorations, including gingerbread houses, sweets and chocolate. While the theme of the 2026 tree is still under wraps, the hotel is already gearing up for Christmas with seasonal cocktails and festive dining experiences. One of London’s most historic and quintessentially English hotels, The Goring is known for its playful approach to Christmas decorations. Last year's tree was created in partnership with British fashion designer Lulu Guinness, whose London Calling installation featured her signature red lips, scarlet ribbons and miniature London postboxes and telephone boxes. While the design of the 2026 tree is still under wraps, the family-owned Belgravia hotel is already gearing up for the festive season, with Christmas dining in its Michelin-starred Dining Room, Champagne-filled celebrations and plenty of seasonal cheer. Art'otel London Hoxton is known for its contemporary approach to art and design, and its Christmas decorations are no exception. Last year's unconventional installation was created by acclaimed artist Shane Keeling, who transformed the traditional Christmas tree into a striking centrepiece made from shattered white porcelain toys, carefully reconstructed and interwoven with festive lights. The hotel has yet to reveal this year's artist, but we're sure the result will be just as spectacular. One of the few hotel Christmas trees in London to stand outside, The Connaught has become something of a festive landmark on Mayfair's Carlos Place. Every year, the hotel commissions a celebrated contemporary artist to reimagine its Christmas tree, and last year's installation was the work of Swiss-born artist Urs Fischer. The 31-foot Nordmann fir was decorated with illuminated spheres containing AI-generated faces, inspired by Fischer’s installation People – first seen in 2022 at Gagosian in New York, with spheres filled with AI-generated faces, each illuminated from within by LED light, evoking people of all ages, races, and places sharing in collective experiences. The artist behind the 2026 tree is yet to be revealed, but it's always one of the capital's most exciting festive displays. The Condé Nast Traveller elves have pulled together the ultimate Christmas lights walking route through the capital for guaranteed glittering illuminations. See our Instagram reel below, along with step-by-step instructions. - Begin with the Regent Street angels and watch as they illuminate one of London’s most famous streets in all their shimmering glory. - From Regent Street, head through Mayfair to Bond Street, where hotels and designer flagships pull out all the stops to illuminate the city’s fanciest shopping destination. - Take a stroll to Fortnum & Mason’s Piccadilly store to see the famous window displays, before looping round to see the iconic Annabel’s members’ club facade. - Fancy maxing out the step count? Take a 35-minute walk (or hop on the Tube) away from the hustle and bustle to Sloane Square, which always gets a fabulous festive makeover. There are plenty more Christmas Lights in London, sure to add some festive cheer to a stroll, many sticking around until the beginning of January. There’s the shooting stars above Oxford Street, the baubles and bells of Covent Garden, and the sparkling tailor's tools of Savile Row to be spotted. Heading through the heart of the city? Keep an eye out for The Shard’s Christmas light display, which transforms the top of London's tallest building into a spectacular illuminated landmark during the festive season. A trip to the theatre has long been a favourite festive pastime of Londoners, as West End theatres receive a sparkly makeover and a series of seasonal shows pop up in beloved fringe theatres. In recent years, various immersive experiences and trails have become increasingly popular, offering an alternative to the traditional theatre experience – ideal for restless little ones. Here are some of the shows and experiences the Condé Nast Traveller editors are most looking forward to this Christmas. For particularly family-friendly outings, head a little further out. This Christmas, Chiswick House is welcoming festive visitors for a heartwarming production of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol, brought to life by Quantum Theatre. Transporting audiences back to Victorian London, the show follows the miserly Ebenezer Scrooge as he encounters four ghostly apparitions on Christmas Eve, who attempt to change his ways before Christmas morning. Taking place in the Garden Pavilion on 21 and 22 December, it's a lovely way to enjoy a traditional Christmas story with the whole family. Address: Chiswick House, Burlington Lane, Chiswick, London W4 2RP Take the children to dance under the snow in Windsor Gardens as The Paddington Bear Experience undergoes a festive makeover from 10 November 2026 to 4 January 2027. Step into Paddington Station, where train masters serve you mince pies under the towering Christmas Tree before whipping you off to help Mrs Brown and Mrs Bird prepare for Marmalade Day. An exciting orange hunt through the Brown household and the Peruvian jungle culminates in hot chocolate and marmalade sandwiches in Windsor Gardens, where you’ll even get to meet everyone’s favourite bear. Jessica Rach Address: The Paddington Bear Experience, Riverside Building, County Hall, Westminster Bridge Rd, London SE1 7PB What's more joyful than a night at ABBA Voyage? A night at ABBA Voyage during Christmastime! Winter at the ABBA Arena features a magical winter garden where guests can gather before the show to drink and dance. The new heated winter bar is a welcome space serving festive-themed cocktails, mulled wine, and cider, and there's festive-themed food on offer too. Superfans will love the additional Christmas-themed merchandise – there's definitely room on your tree for an ABBA Voyage bauble. Abigail Malbon Address: ABBA Arena, 1 Pudding Mill Lane, London E15 2RU There are few Christmas traditions quite as magical as a trip to see The Nutcracker. This winter, English National Ballet returns to the London Coliseum with its spectacular production of the Tchaikovsky classic, following Clara on a journey through a world of dancing snowflakes, enchanted toys and the Kingdom of Sweets. Expect beautiful costumes, elaborate sets and some of the most recognisable music in ballet. Running from 17 December 2026 to 10 January 2027, it's the perfect excuse to dress up, head into the West End and make a proper festive evening of it. Alessia Armenise Address: London Coliseum, St Martin's Lane, London WC2N 4ES Dickens' A Christmas Carol is practically synonymous with Christmas in London, and The Old Vic's much-loved adaptation has become something of a festive tradition in its own right. Adapted by Jack Thorne, the production brings Ebenezer Scrooge's journey from miserly old businessman to generous Christmas enthusiast to life through atmospheric staging, traditional carols and plenty of audience participation. Returning for its tenth consecutive season, from 12 November 2026 to 9 January 2027, it's a heartwarming choice for anyone who loves a good Christmas story. Alessia Armenise Address: The Old Vic, 103 The Cut, London SE1 8NB For Harry Potter fans, Christmas doesn't get much better than seeing Hogwarts covered in snow. From 14 November 2026 to 17 January 2027, Warner Bros. Studio Tour London receives its annual festive makeover, with Christmas trees, decorations and wintry scenes transforming some of the films' most recognisable sets. Wander through the decorated Great Hall, discover how the filmmakers created realistic snow and marvel at the magnificent Hogwarts Castle model in its winter setting. This year's experience also features a Wizard's Chess scene, adding another reason for returning visitors to make the journey just outside London. Alessia Armenise Address: Warner Bros. Studio Tour London, Studio Tour Drive, Leavesden, WD25 7LR Looking for something a little different? Hampton Court Palace is getting a festive makeover this winter, with Winter Palace, a new experience bringing a touch of seasonal magic to the former royal residence. Expect mythical beasts, an enchanted ball and plenty of theatrical flourishes as visitors explore the historic rooms. Running from 28 November 2026 to 3 January 2027, the experience is included with standard palace admission, making it an excellent excuse to spend a winter afternoon exploring one of London's most spectacular historic buildings. Alessia Armenise Address: Hampton Court Palace, East Molesey, Surrey KT8 9AU Looking for something a little quirkier? Each year, stars of stage, screen (and miscellaneous origin) take to the stage in some of London's most storied theatres for tongue-in-cheek takes on fairytale classics. Among the pantomimes to look out for in 2026 are Cinderella at the London Palladium and another take on the same classic at Lyric Hammersmith, alongside Jack and the Beanstalk at Hackney Empire. Expect outrageous costumes, plenty of audience participation and more than a few jokes aimed squarely at the adults in the room.

item.title: Allegiant adds 11 new routes alongside merger partner Sun Country, swaps 5 others
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy
Leisure carrier Allegiant is growing again, this time teaming up with merger partner Sun Country to grow its network. The Las Vegas-based budget airline announced 11 new routes on Tuesday, with the service split between Allegiant and Sun Country. Additionally, five routes will switch from one airline to the other — a tangible sign of the integration that’s slowly getting underway since the acquisition closed earlier this year. New routes from Allegiant and Sun Country The big winner in Tuesday’s announcement: Gulf Shores, Alabama. The Gulf Coast destination — which Allegiant began flying to in 2025 — landed four new routes with Allegiant as well as one new route with Sun Country. It’s a remarkable ramp for the Gulf Shores International Airport at Jack Edwards Field (GUF), which now has nonstop flights to 17 destinations, according to the airport’s website. The airport had no regular airline service at all prior to Allegiant’s arrival. When Sun Country’s new service to Minneapolis-Saint Paul International Airport (MSP) begins April 16, it will mark the first time an airline other than Allegiant has scheduled service from the airport. Elsewhere, Allegiant added two new Florida routes from the mid-Atlantic: one each from Philadelphia and Washington, D.C. Sun Country will add nonstop service from O’Hare International Airport (ORD) to Asheville, North Carolina, and Knoxville, Tennessee — two destinations near the Great Smoky Mountains National Park that are already served by Allegiant. Beyond the new routes, Allegiant is poised to take over service on four routes currently operated by Sun Country. Meanwhile, Sun Country will assume Allegiant’s Cincinnati-Denver route on May 27. The changes will effectively add three new destinations to Sun Country's network: Belleville, Illinois, near St. Louis; Gulf Shores, Alabama; and Knoxville, Tennessee. Meanwhile, MSP — Sun Country's home base and main hub — will join Allegiant's route map. "Minnesota is an essential part of the future of our combined company, and today's announcement is another step in delivering on that commitment," Allegiant CEO Greg Anderson said in a statement. "MSP is our largest base of operations by a wide margin, and we see opportunities for continued growth there." Allegiant and Sun Country will continue to operate as separate brands at least into 2028 “or later,” Allegiant said in the press release. It will eventually move to a single brand. For now, however, Allegiant touted Tuesday’s new service announcement as a preview of the expanded network that customers of the combined carrier will eventually be able to access. "As we planned for summer 2027, our focus was on creating more opportunities for travelers by leveraging the complementary strengths of each airline's network while continuing to operate separately," Drew Wells, Allegiant's chief commercial officer, said in the company's statement. “Just as importantly, these routes are a first look at how we'll create more options, access and value for our customers in the long term,” he added.
