item.title: INSTRUCTION: Maple-Glazed Carrots
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
These maple-glazed carrots don’t hold back on the butter—or the brown sugar. Roasted with pure maple syrup and crushed red pepper flakes, they turn tender and glossy with a sweet-hot kick that complements everything from ham to lamb to green bean casserole. The recipe began with Barbie—not the doll, but Andy Baraghani’s cousin’s former girlfriend. Her syrupy-sweet carrots became a fixture at family Christmas dinners. Some dishes are meant to last; some relationships aren’t. For BA’s version, Andy traded the original’s hours-long cooking time for a hotter roast that gives the carrots browned edges and a buttery glaze. There’s no separate sauce to simmer: Everything goes straight onto a foil-lined (for easier cleanup) rimmed baking sheet, with regular tossing to coat the carrots in syrup as they cook. Finish with flaky salt for crunch and a welcome contrast to the sweetness. Do I need to peel the carrots? No. This recipe calls for scrubbed, unpeeled carrots—give them a thorough cleaning and leave the skins on. How do I keep the glaze from burning? Keep the carrot pieces similar in thickness, halving or quartering larger ones lengthwise. Check the glaze each time you toss the carrots, especially once the edges begin browning: The sugars can darken quickly. Use tenderness and browned edges as your guide rather than waiting out the clock if the carrots are already done. For a more savory version, try our Easy Roasted Carrots. Need to make a substitution? - Step 1Place rack in middle of oven and preheat oven to 400°. Line a rimmed baking sheet with 3 sheets of foil (you’ll need it!). Cut 2 lb. medium carrots, tops trimmed to about ½", scrubbed, on a diagonal into 3" pieces (halved or quartered lengthwise if large). Step 2Spread out carrots on foil. Evenly top with 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, cut into pieces, ⅓ cup (packed; 70 g) light brown sugar, ⅓ cup pure maple syrup, and ¾ tsp. crushed red pepper flakes. Season with kosher salt and toss to combine. Step 3Roast carrots, tossing every 20 minutes, until tender and browned around the edges, 50–60 minutes. Watch closely as the carrots begin to brown; the glaze can darken quickly. Transfer to a platter and drizzle with any remaining syrup. Sprinkle with flaky sea salt (if using). Editor’s note: This recipe for maple carrots was first published in November 2018; it has been updated for clarity and style. Head this way for more of our best carrot recipes →

item.title: INSTRUCTION: BA's Best Pecan Pie
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
Our classic pecan pie recipe has no chocolate chips, no booze, and no hard-to-find ingredients. Instead of focusing on embellishments, we focused on what matters most: the deep flavor of toasted pecans, a caramelly custard, and a buttery, flaky pie crust. Brown sugar and a spoonful of dark molasses add depth to the filling, while toasting the pecans before incorporating them makes their flavor stand out and their texture more robust. Blind baking the crust—baking it before adding the filling—helps keep the bottom crisp beneath the gooey custard. When the pie comes out of the oven, the edges should be set and slightly puffed, but the center should still wobble like Jell-O. It will continue to set as it cools, so resist slicing too soon. Serve it all on its own, or gild it with vanilla ice cream or whipped cream. Can I make this pecan pie without corn syrup? Yes. Corn syrup gives this classic pie its perfectly gooey texture, but there are alternatives. Brown rice syrup will add a toasty flavor and can be used in equal parts. Golden syrup, honey, and maple syrup are all too sweet and will change the pie’s flavor and texture. For a pie developed without any syrup, try our Bourbon-Date Pecan Pie. Can I use chopped pecans instead of halves? Yes. We love the crunch you get from pecan halves, but if you’re a chopped pecan person, use about 225 g in place of the 2 cups of halves. Watch closely when toasting; chopped pecans will need less time in the oven. Can I make pecan pie ahead of time? Yes—bake the pie a day ahead and refrigerate it. Let it cool on a rack for up to 2 hours, then transfer it to the refrigerator to finish cooling before covering. To get a head start on the pastry, refrigerate the dough for up to 3 days or freeze it for up to 2 months. Need to make a substitution? - CrustStep 1Pulse 1 Tbsp. sugar, 1½ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ¾ tsp. Morton kosher salt, and 2 cups all-purpose flour in a food processor until combined. Add 5 Tbsp. chilled unsalted butter, cut into pieces, and 3 Tbsp. chilled lard or vegetable shortening and pulse until mixture resembles coarse meal with a few pieces of butter and lard visible, about fifteen 1-second pulses. With motor running, drizzle in 1 Tbsp. apple cider vinegar and 5½ Tbsp. ice water and pulse until dough is still crumbly but just holds together when squeezed (add 1 tsp. water at a time if necessary, but be careful not to overwork dough). Step 2Turn out dough onto a work surface. Knead 1–2 times, pressing just to incorporate any shaggy pieces. Flatten into a 6"-wide disk. Wrap with plastic wrap and chill at least 1 hour. Step 3Preheat oven to 425°. Roll out dough on a lightly floured work surface to a 14" round. Transfer to a 9" pie pan. Pick up edges and allow dough to slump down into dish, letting excess dough hang over dish. Trim, leaving about a 1" overhang. Fold overhang under; pinch and crimp. Chill 30 minutes. Step 4Line dough with parchment paper or foil, leaving some overhang. Fill with pie weights or dried beans. Bake until crust is dry around the edges and just beginning to lightly brown, 25–35 minutes. Carefully remove parchment and weights and reduce oven temperature to 350°. Bake until crust is set and beginning to brown in the center, 10–15 minutes. Transfer to a wire rack and let cool. Do Ahead: Dough can be made 3 days ahead; keep chilled, or freeze up to 2 months. Crust can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and store at room temperature. - Filling and AssemblyStep 5Preheat oven to 350°. Toast 2 cups (225 g) pecan halves on a rimmed baking sheet until browned and fragrant, 8–10 minutes. Let cool. Step 6Reduce oven temperature to 325°. Whisk 4 large eggs, room temperature, beaten to blend, 1 cup light corn syrup, ⅔ cup (packed; 134 g) light brown sugar, 1 Tbsp. robust-flavored (dark) molasses, 1 Tbsp. vanilla extract, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Slowly whisk in 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, until combined. Fold in pecans and pour into cooled crust. Step 7Bake pie until edges are set and slightly puffed but center is recessed and wobbles like Jell-O, 55–70 minutes (it will continue to set after baking). Transfer to a wire rack and let cool at least 3 hours before slicing. Serve with vanilla ice cream. Do Ahead: Pie can be baked 1 day ahead; tightly wrap and chill. Serve warm or at room temperature. Editor’s note: This pecan pie recipe was first published in November 2016 and has been updated for style. For more of our best pie recipes, head this way →

item.title: Giant November Waves Threaten Surfers, Swimmers, and Spectators Along California’s Coast
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine
Powerful waves crash against Pacifica Pier in Pacifica, California, on November 14, 2026, as large Pacific swells batter the state's coastline. (Photo: Stephen Lam/San Francisco Chronicle via Getty Images) Lifeguards along California’s coast have had their hands full over the past several days, as powerful Pacific swells stranded surfers, swept a teenager photographing the waves off rocks, and even overturned a rescue jet ski during an operation near Santa Cruz. In San Diego alone, lifeguards conducted 175 water rescues between November 9 and 16, according to San Diego Fire-Rescue figures reported by FOX 5/KUSI. “I’ve seen seasons start off with a bang like this, but we’ve never had this type of impact so immediate,” Ernst Bauen, operations division chief for the Central Fire District of Santa Cruz County, told Outside on November 17. The enormous swells were generated by powerful low-pressure systems over the northeastern Pacific, where hurricane-force winds pushed waves toward the California coast, according to the National Weather Service. On November 14, forecasters predicted breaking waves of 25 to 35 feet, with occasional sets reaching 40 to 50 feet at big-wave surfing spot Mavericks, near Half Moon Bay. Bauen, who spent about 20 years as a rescue swimmer, said waves are reaching roads, cliffs, and beach access points earlier in the season than usual. “The ocean is extremely dynamic, and where there used to be a safe amount of space to recreate even on the beach, those spaces are becoming fewer and further between because of the erosion along our coastline,” he said. On November 14, rescue crews pulled three surfers from the water near Pleasure Point in Santa Cruz County. A fire department rescuer had picked up two surfers on a jet ski when a large wave overturned the watercraft, throwing all three into the ocean. The rescuer, a part of Bauen’s team, managed to right the jet ski and continue the operation, returning about ten minutes later to help a third surfer. Hundreds of miles south that same day, a San Diego lifeguard swam through powerful breaking waves to reach a struggling swimmer at La Jolla Cove. Another lifeguard eventually arrived on a jet ski and brought both men to safety. Also in San Diego on November 14, at nearby Windansea Beach, a teenager photographing the waves from nearby rocks was swept into the ocean. A surfer jumped into the water and briefly helped keep the teenager’s head above the surface before waves carried him toward the rocky shoreline, where several bystanders helped pull him out. The close call underscored warnings from San Diego Lifeguard Chief Daniel Orloff that even spectators watching from dry land were at risk. “If you are close, at any moment, a wave could take you out. It can breach a bluff, a berm, even the boardwalk,” he told ABC 10News. In Orange County, a surfer helped rescue three people struggling in strong currents at Crystal Cove State Beach on November 15, according to a witness who shared video of the aftermath with TV station 10 News San Diego. Not every incident ended in a rescue. On November 14, a man disappeared while swimming near Zuma Beach in Malibu. Lifeguards responded to the scene around 1:40 p.m., and Coast Guard helicopters and boat crews searched for the missing swimmer into the following day. The Coast Guard suspended its search on November 15 without locating him. The man has not publicly been identified. Bauen said the ocean can also lull people into a false sense of security. During these swells, waves can stay relatively small for 15 or 20 minutes at a time, making conditions look calm before a surge of much larger waves suddenly arrives and catches surfers off guard. Rising tides can also leave surfers stranded when the beach access points they used to enter the water become submerged. While the largest waves have eased, forecasters say hazardous surf will linger through November 19. In its November 17 forecast, the National Weather Service predicted breaking waves of 13 to 17 feet along portions of the Bay Area and Central Coast through November 18, with dangerous rip currents and sneaker waves. Bauen urged surfers and beachgoers to check the forecast, pay attention to changing conditions, and identify a safe route back to shore before entering the water. “Ultimately, it comes down to the individual,” Bauen said. “You really need to know before you go. You need to tune into the ocean conditions, look up forecasts, and do a little bit of research before you explore a secluded beach, decide to go for a swim, or paddle out.”

item.title: Art exhibitions in Paris for November 2026: from Musée du Luxembourg to La Collection at Musée National Picasso
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
With November blustering through the streets of Paris, the city’s museums and galleries settle into a rich season of long-running and unmissable exhibitions. Many of them are running until early 2027, offering ample opportunity for a visit. Several are so provocative and beguiling that you may want to experience them twice. Heavyweight names on the contemporary art scene such as Kerry James Marshall and David Hockney rub shoulders with the timeless masters like Tintoretto and Cézanne. Complementing this round-up of blockbuster shows, Paris never fails to delight with its permanent collections. Monet’s water lilies at the Musée de l’Orangerie are the perfect antidote to gloomy, grey skies, while the Musée Rodin and its expansive gardens dotted with sculpted masterpieces invite a slow stroll on those crispiest of winter days. We update this column monthly so that you can always follow the best upcoming exhibitions in Paris. The luminous museum La Galerie Dior is described as “a place of art and memory” and celebrates Parisian couture and the heritage of the iconic brand. Monsieur Dior was originally a gallerist and was continually inspired by art and architecture as both a collector and designer. The brand continues to be involved in art. The visionary creative director, Maria Grazia Chiuri, has always ensured that inspiring women are perpetually at the forefront of their leadership and vision at Dior. Experience their history through exquisite archival sketches, photographs and original looks as well as sources of inspiration from the artistic to the botanical. Address: 11 Rue François 1er, 75008 Paris 2. Claude Monet’s Water Lilies at Musée de l'Orangerie One of the most beautiful corners of the city is the Musée de l'Orangerie, built alongside the Jeu de Paume in the Jardin des Tuileries. It is synonymous with the hypnotic Water Lilies (Les Nymphéas), a series of eight extended canvases by Claude Monet, which were generously donated to the French state after WWI as a symbol of peace. As with Monet’s studio in Giverny, natural light floods into the galleries and illuminates the paintings. Address: Jardin des Tuileries, 75001 Paris Price: From €12.50; concessions available 3. La Collection at Musée National Picasso-Paris Housed inside the opulent 17th-century Hôtel Salé, the opulent Musée National Picasso-Paris is devoted to the Spanish master and the artists with whom he collaborated. Over 5,000 works are held within its collection, spread across sumptuous hallways and lofty, light-filled rooms, including preparatory sketches as well as his abundant photographic archive, poetry and correspondence. The museum is located on the picturesque Rue de Thorigny in Le Marais, near smaller worthwhile galleries like Perrotin and David Zwirner. Complementing its hefty permanent collection, the museum’s major temporary exhibition is dedicated to the prolific career of German-born artist, Kurt Schwitters – thirty years after France last dedicated a retrospective to him. Though Schwitters’ active years aligned with the Dada movement, Constructivism and Abstraction, his work doesn’t fit neatly into any of these categories. A painter, poet, musician, sculptor, typographer, magazine editor and event organiser, Schwitters built a world entirely of his own, which he called ‘Merz.’ This exhibition titled ‘Le Chaos-Monde 1918-1948’ traces his undefinable oeuvre. Bringing together a collection of over three hundred works and archival documents, it ultimately affirms his legacy as one of modern art’s great lone wolves. Dates: Permanent collection until 12 March 2027; ‘Kurt Schwitters, Le Chaos Monde 1918-1948’ until 7th February 2027 Only a short walk from the Eiffel Tower and Grand Palais, Musée Rodin was opened in 1919 and has since been devoted to the work of the prolific French Sculptor Auguste Rodin. Get lost in the classical architecture with exquisite rocaille details. The sculpture garden is also exquisite and offers a quiet escape during the summer months. The museum featured in Midnight in Paris, directed by Woody Allen. Carla Bruni had a cameo as a tour guide. From 11 September, Musée Jacquemart-André - one of Paris’ most beautiful mansion-museums – will immerse its visitors into the sumptuous world of Jacopo Tintoretto, a leading figure of 16th-century Italian Mannerism. This will be the artist’s first major French retrospective, whose bold, vibrant, and at times controversial paintings were well ahead of their time. Based in Venice, Tintoretto made a name for himself through large-scale public commissions of the city’s most prestigious buildings. In this exhibition, forty rare paintings and works on paper are brought together from both public and private collections worldwide, with the aim of illuminating Tintoretto’s remarkable and widespread talent, and an oeuvre that firmly defies categorisation. Kerry James Marshall is undeniably one of the most influential painters of our time, cementing his legacy in France’s first exhibition devoted to his work. Alongside his curatorial involvement, the Musée d’Art Moderne de Paris brings together 70 works, including eight which were specifically created for this exhibition. They showcase the artist’s thoughtful and confronting oeuvre, which glorifies the mundane everyday and insists on the power of presence. Rooms are arranged thematically, tracing Marshall’s earliest engagements with the underrepresentation of the Black figure in museum spaces. He expands on this crux, which occupies his entire career with later paintings that tackle the American Civil Rights movement and the transatlantic slave trade. In a poignant nod to its Parisian setting, several works on display reference artists such as Manet and Seurat, exposing as well as linking the history of art into Marshall’s pictorial voice. Website: 11 Avenue du Président Wilson, 75116 Paris The Bourse de Commerce’s historic rotunda has, by now, gained icon status with its installations that encourage visitors to become a part of the spectacle. While its latest exhibition returns to a more analogue medium of art, it is no less immersive. Marking the bicentenary of the invention of photography, the Pinault Collection gathers more than 700 works by over 70 artists to diligently trace the evolution of the camera. Rather than opt for a chronological curation, viewers are encouraged to form their own journey through the images and form individual connections and dialogues. A conscious effort to showcase extraordinary breadth places early 19th-century daguerreotypes alongside contemporary masterpieces by the likes of Wolfgang Tillmans, Lee Miller and Cindy Sherman. The pinnacle of the show takes place in the rotunda with an installation by Barbara Kruger whose titular work Remember Me lends its name to the entire exhibition. Andy Warhol’s cult icon status and instantly recognisable oeuvre is a double-edged sword. While it solidifies his position as one of the most famous artists in modern history, it can make it difficult to find fresh ways to be surprised by his ubiquitous screen prints. Enter the Musée du Luxembourg, who tackle this challenge head-on with an exhibition dedicated to Warhol’s lesser-known yet deeply important works on paper. They have collated nearly 150 line drawings complemented by paintings, photographs and archival documents in order to demonstrate the Pop Artist’s delicate process of draftsmanship, invention and seriality. This is a captivating new perspective on a figure that everyone feels they know, yet few have seen through this lens. Address: 19, rue de Vaugirard, 75006, Paris As one of the most widely recognised figures in the history of modern art, it is easy to forget that Paul Cézanne almost fell into obscurity. It was only towards the end of his lifetime at the turn of the 20th century that critics and collectors began to grasp the true radicalism of his vision. Since then, his structural brushwork has influenced generations of avant-garde artists including Peter Doig, Bridget Riley, Pablo Picasso, and Piet Mondrian to name just a few. At the Grand Palais, Cézanne and Us unpacks this seminal painter’s own complex biography while also demonstrating how his canvases acted as a springboard for a remarkably diverse group of subsequent artists. The exhibition goes well beyond mere aesthetic connections as it also interrogates Cézanne’s controversial reputation as the true “father of modern art.” Address: 17 Avenue du Général Eisenhower, 75008 10. Histories of Landscape, from Monet to Hockney (1890 - 2026) The year 2026 marks a century since Claude Monet’s death, making the inauguration of this new exhibition particularly poignant. The Musée Marmottan Monet unites works by Monet, David Hockney and a century of other artists in between them through the lens of landscape painting. Although the last 100 years saw world wars, mass modernisation and rapid technological acceleration, this show demonstrates the enduring relevance and resilience of the natural world, especially in the face of great upheaval. It opens with a painting of two water lilies which Monet bestowed upon the French nation after the Armistice of 11 November 1918 and continues to evolve with a focus on the vibrant and often tense boundary between nature and artifice. To mark the opening of Fondation Cartier pour l’art contemporain’s new Parisian space, an exhibition of monumental proportion was needed to claim the inaugural spot. Ghanaian artist Ibrahim Mahama takes the stand, alongside nine associate artists and collectives specially chosen by him. Across Mahama’s varied and ambitious oeuvre, the running thread has always been an intent to democratise access to art. This showcase in Paris is a reflection of his work in Tamale, northern Ghana, where he has founded several art centres in order to nurture local talent. His work at once celebrates and interrogates the minutiae of his Ghanaian origins while also connecting them to wider themes in the cultural, social, political and creative spheres. At the Fondation Cartier, a host of site-specific installations fill the lofty rooms. Among them is Mahama’s latest project – the Aboso Glass Factory – which acts as an artwork and learning space. Alongside the contributions from his carefully selected group of artists, Mahama celebrates the exchange of knowledge, ideas, and artistic pursuit while shining the spotlight on the Ghanaian art scene in conjunction with further creative hubs across the globe. Address: 2, place du Palais-Royal, 75001 Website: https://www.fondationcartier.com/en

item.title: REVIEW: My favourite stay: a design-led Florentine apartment that feels like your own private palazzo
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK
Florence has been part of my life for as long as I can remember. My father worked in fashion and would fly in for the menswear fair Pitti Uomo. I would tag along too, sitting in on meetings and watching him pore over fabrics and lookbooks. My dear friend Gaby has also called Florence home for many years, so I find myself returning whenever I can. I love that it is charmingly small, yet feels like an epicentre of fashion, food, wine, art and design. You can cross the city on foot in an afternoon, but its influence stretches around the world. On my latest trip, I stayed at Palazzo Ottaviani, home to immaculately designed apartments just moments from the Basilica di Santa Maria Novella. Part of the Lungarno Collection, the Italian hotel and apartment group owned by Florentine fashion dynasty, the Ferragamo family, it gave me the chance to live out my Firenze flat dream. Housed in a 1950s building that has had many guises, including that of the city's storied Ariston Cinema, it has undergone an impeccable renovation and now comprises a welcome area and ten apartments of different sizes, including a penthouse with a panoramic terrace. The Palazzo was born from the vision of the Marquis of San Giuliano, who married Fiamma Ferragamo, the daughter of Salvatore Ferragamo. He spent almost four decades creating one of Europe’s most extensive miniature railway systems. His collection now lives on at Hzero, the museum on the ground floor, while their children continue his vision for the Palazzo. We stayed in a two-bedroom apartment with a generous living room and the moment we stepped through the door, I knew this was no ordinary Airbnb. We were greeted by a vase of flowers along with biscuits and jams from Giardino San Giuliano estate, the family farm in Sicily. The design is fabulously chic, with impressive craftsmanship throughout. Luigi Fragola Architects, the studio behind some of the city’s most prestigious addresses, took inspiration from the clean geometry of 1940s Rationalism and the glamour of Art Deco, with tailored textiles, large-scale works by local artists and flashes of blue and gold. Everything felt very thoughtfully considered, from the finishes to the furniture; a haven of deep wood and dark marble. Our apartment also had a stylish kitchen with everything needed for a few days. The bathrooms were works of art, one had a deep marble tub overlooking the street below. With Mercato Centrale just a few minutes’ walk away, it was easy to stock up on delicious local produce and bring it back to enjoy at home. Each morning, pistachio and cream croissants appeared at our door which, paired with a strong espresso, made a rather lovely start to the day. During our stay the penthouse was unoccupied, so I asked for a sneak peek of the rooftop. It was vast, with a picturesque outlook over the neighbouring Florentine rooftops, and made for a wonderful spot to pause and take in the city. There is something about those terracotta roofs stretching out towards the hills that never gets old. The location is a big draw. Palazzo Ottaviani is on Via del Palazzuolo, within easy walking distance of many of Florence's greatest sights. Staying somewhere so central makes it easy to dip in and out of the city rather than feeling as though you are constantly sightseeing. Florence can be busy and intense, but after a day spent walking around galleries, shops and piazzas, it was lovely to come back to somewhere that felt so calm and considered. The concierge team is also always at hand, whether you need a restaurant recommendation, help booking dinner or a little local intel on where to go next. Being part of the Lungarno Collection means you can make the most of its sister properties, including Portrait Firenze, one of my favourite places to drop into for aperitivo. The hotel has a wonderfully intimate atmosphere, with a team that will make you feel welcome whether you are staying the night or not. The pièce de résistance is its incredible River View suite overlooking the Ponte Vecchio, which I have been fortunate enough to spend the night in. It has one of the most iconic views in Florence, taking in the river and the bridge below, with the city unfolding on either side. I would recommend dinner at Caffè dell'Oro, where lovely Chef Luca Armellino heads up the food. His mix of Italian cuisine with an international twist is something refreshingly different (red shrimp toastada and fregola with scallop are musts). Not to mention the setting, with an extraordinary view of the Ponte Vecchio. Our booking at Palazzo Ottaviani also included complimentary entry to the Ferragamo Museum and the child-friendly Hzero miniature railway museum, which was another perk of staying within the collection. Palazzo Ottaviani offers the service of a luxury hotel, with the space, privacy and comfort of a very beautiful Florentine home. Let’s just say, if I could have my pick of fashion apartments to stay at for Pitti Uomo, this would be it.

item.title: Behind the Scenes of the Inaugural Bon Appétit LIVE
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
This past weekend the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen in New York City opened its doors to the public for Bon Appétit Live, an immersive day of cooking demos and classes, talks with chefs and recipe experts, Test Kitchen tours, games, prizes, and plenty to eat and drink. The day kicked off with a warm welcome from Bon Appétit’s editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, who exclaimed that “the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen is the heart of our brand.” Robinson also shared that Bon Appétit just launched a new cooking app containing tens of thousands of recipes from the Test Kitchen archives. Guests fueled up with an impressive array of curated breakfast treats alongside refreshing beverages from S.Pellegrino, before moving on to interactive experiences. In the first class of the day, baking novices and aficionados alike joined senior Test Kitchen editor and BA Bake Club expert Jesse Szewczyk in the Test Kitchen for Pie Crust Fundamentals, presented by East Fork. The hands-on class featured guest Keia Mastrianni, brand storyteller and “unofficial pie lady” of East Fork. Mastrianni proclaimed her enthusiasm for pie making: “I love preaching the gospel of pie. My favorite thing is teaching people to make pie dough with their hands.” Szewczyk agreed, emphasizing the tactile nature of the process: “It’s a very physical thing to do…a recipe can be written, but teaching someone to make pie dough requires demonstration.” Participants were in luck as Szewczyk and Mastrianni demonstrated a buttery pie crust fortified with cream cheese, a recipe ideal for Thanksgiving developed by former senior Test Kitchen editor Shilpa Uskokovic. After Mastrianni shared crimping tips, participants made their own pie dough at stations throughout the kitchen, with Test Kitchen editors on hand to offer guidance. One participant, James, was particularly excited to be working with director of cooking Emma Laperruque. He enthused, “Before Emma’s and Chris [Morocco’s] recipes, I would burn water. [Bon Appétit] has made cooking really accessible, and I built a lot of confidence. I love the simplicity of Emma’s recipes…they are all so flavorful and so good.” Each guest left ready for holiday baking season with new pie-making skills, and a ceramic pie dish from East Fork’s new bakeware collection, featuring clay and glaze made in-house with materials sourced in the Southeast. Before moving on to their next experience, Mastrianni encouraged everyone to keep honing their skills, emphasizing, “Practice makes pie. Progress, not perfection.” Meanwhile, in the neighboring Demo Kitchen, a Pasta Boot Camp was underway with Bon Appétit senior cooking editor Kelsey Jane Youngman and chef Stefano Secchi. Secchi, chef and partner of New York City’s Rezdôra (recipient of one Michelin star) and Massara, honed his craft in Modena, Italy, under legendary chef Massimo Bottura. After walking guests through the fundamentals of making and shaping fresh pasta by hand, Secchi demonstrated a filled ravioli dish aptly named Holiday in Parma. Made with 00 flour and egg dough, the ravioli was piped with a chestnut and Parmesan filling and served with a rich reduction of chicken broth, butter, and saba (a traditional Italian syrup made from slowly simmered grape must). While guests savored their pasta in the Demo Kitchen, a lively panel discussion was underway on the 34th floor. Moderated by editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson, the Bringing Culture to Cooking panel featured chefs Fariyal Abdullahi (executive chef, Hav & Mar, NYC), Nicholas Bazik (chef and owner, Provenance, Philadelphia, a Bon Appétit Best New Restaurant of 2025), and Vijay Kumar (executive chef and partner, Semma, NYC, a Best New Restaurant of 2022). The conversation explored how culture, identity, and personal experience inform each chef’s cooking. The chefs shared some of their favorite home-cooking ingredients, such as Chef Bazik’s fermented lime juice, a versatile seasoning made by combining fresh lime juice with salt at a 2% ratio by weight. Chef Abdullahi championed berbere, the Ethiopian spice blend she likened to “Ethiopian salt” for its ubiquity in the country’s cooking. Abdullahi cautioned that store-bought blends are convenient but not necessarily of the highest-possible quality. “You should make it at home!” she encouraged. Back in the Test Kitchen, Visit Maine hosted Lobster 101, a hands-on lobster class and oyster tasting with Bon Appétit’s manager of audience strategy Carly Westerfield and Krista Tripp, founder of Aphrodite Oysters in South Thomaston, Maine. Each participant received a whole, steamed Maine lobster and the ingredients and tools needed to transform it into a creamy, decadent lobster dip. Under Westerfield’s guidance, the class learned how to break down their lobsters, extract the meat, and assemble a dip made with cream cheese, mayonnaise, celery, chives, and lemon juice. The approachable demonstration demystified the process and showed guests how easily they could prepare a luxurious appetizer at home, just in time for the holidays. Participants worked with hard-shell lobsters, but Tripp encouraged them to visit Maine and sample both hard-shell and soft-shell varieties. She explained that soft-shell lobsters, typically in season from July through August, have a sweeter, more tender meat. The two are actually the same animal at different stages of its molting cycle: a soft-shell lobster has recently shed its old shell, leaving a newer, more pliable one that is easier to crack. The class concluded with a tasting of Aphrodite Oysters, grown in the waters off South Thomaston, Maine. The medium-size oysters were briny and subtly sweet, reflecting the cold, brackish waters of the Lower Weskeag River where they were grown. A small squeeze of lemon was all that was needed to enhance their flavor as guests tilted their heads back, slurped, and allowed themselves to be transported to the rugged coast of Maine. Meanwhile, in the Demo Kitchen, Bon Appétit director of culture Joseph Hernandez was joined by Matt Conroy, chef at Washington, DC’s Maison Bar à Vins, for a live cooking demonstration of one of Chef Conroy’s favorite dishes. Named one of Bon Appétit’s Best New Restaurants of 2026, the restaurant pairs French-inspired cooking with an eclectic wine list and seasonal cocktails. Chef Conroy prepared a new fall salad made of chicory, pear, and smoked blue cheese, finished with a Banyuls vinaigrette. In the cafeteria, guests gathered for a live version of the Dear Bon Appétit advice column. Bon Appétit director of cooking Emma Laperruque presented questions about home cooking and holiday entertaining to chef Amanda Freitag. One attendee asked Freitag how to handle undercooked turkey legs and thighs each year. Freitag recommended removing the legs and cooking them separately, as in this BA recipe for Gravy-Braised Turkey from Jesse Szewczyk. Next, food stylist Thu Buser showcased her exceptional culinary artistry by decorating an elaborate “snake cake” with vibrant green swirls and flowers. Then, a break for lunch with BA’s Best Mozzarella Sticks, a variety of salads and skewers, hot honey salmon, smoothies, and a cranberry maple mule. While attendees grazed and mingled, Jamila Robinson joined legendary chef and restaurateur Marcus Samuelsson to discuss Back to Green: Rediscovering a World of Delicious, Healthy Eating, his new global plant-forward cookbook coauthored by Robinson. Samuelsson captured the atmosphere of the event, remarking, “What a party we are having here…the energy is amazing!” The final demonstration of the day featured Cornmeal Shortcakes with Blueberry Compote presented by Visit Maine with Jesse Szewczyk and Ron Howard of Brodis Blueberries. Featuring a recipe from Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firsker, the shortcakes showcased farm-fresh wild blueberries grown on a ninth-generation family farm. As Szewczyk prepared the recipe, Howard discussed the importance of wild blueberries to Maine’s agricultural heritage. A native crop, they can be traced back to the end of the last Ice Age, predating lobster as a symbol of the state. “Everyone should think of wild blueberries as the ultimate Maine crop,” Howard explained. After tasting the shortcakes, attendees would be hard-pressed to disagree. Szewczyk noted that compared with conventional blueberries, the wild blueberries produced a more saturated color and tasted more distinctly of blueberry. The day ended on a sweet note with pastry chef Eunji Lee, winner of North America’s Best Pastry Chef Award from The 50. Attendees had a chance to meet Lee and sample pastries from Lysée, her pastry boutique influenced by Korean and French culture and inspired by New York City. Bon Appétit Live brought together chefs, culinary personalities, and food editors for a day of conversations, cooking, tasting, and learning. Attendees experienced the Bon Appétit Test Kitchen firsthand, learned directly from chefs and editors, and engaged with the people and products behind the food. As editor-in-chief Jamila Robinson said, “Food is always an invitation…we are so happy to give everyone access to the same experiences we have.” Bon Appétit LIVE 2026 was sponsored by East Fork, Visit Maine, and S.Pellegrino® Sparkling Natural Mineral Water with thanks to All-Clad, As Ever, Bachan’s, Better Sour, Field Company, Floura, Gimme Seaweed, GOODLES, Graza, Hedley & Bennett, Kann Coffee, Material Kitchen, Misen, Owala®, Rip Van, SharkNinja, and Staub.

item.title: REVIEW: Naomi Hand Scrub Gets Rid of Garlic Smells and Softens Your Skin
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit
I’m a big proponent of indulging in little luxuries—especially if they’re for my home, where I live and work. I acquire fresh flowers weekly, I don’t wait for special occasions to burn expensive candles, and my hand soap smells like it came from a fancy hotel. Until very recently, I kept my luxuriously scented soaps in both my bathroom and my kitchen. The latter, I realize, isn't the most practical choice—after cutting onions or garlic, a pleasant fragrance doesn’t so much mask the smell as combine with it. But sticking a pump bottle of Dial or SoftSoap next to my sink doesn’t exactly fit the bougie-divorcée apartment vibe I’m going for. Now I don’t have to choose because somebody finally developed fancy hand soap just for cooks. And it’s really nice. Naomi After-Cooking Hand Scrub is the creation of an enthusiastic home cook whose girlfriend couldn’t stand the garlic smell that lingered on his hands. Like me, she also happened to have a thing for premium hand soaps. And I’m so glad she did because this stuff really is a dream. The selling point for anyone who regularly chops alliums is that it uses bread yeast enzymes to neutralize odors. It also exfoliates your hands with tiny (though not uncomfortable) pieces of volcanic rock and keeps your skin soft with olive oil esters. But the thing that has me swooning is the fragrance: a combination of bergamot, sandalwood, and black pepper. It’s subtle but feels rich, and I prefer it to Aesop’s Resurrection Hand Wash. Naomi’s After-Cooking Hand Scrub happens to be about half the price of Aesop’s Hand Wash too. Before I finished my first bottle, I ordered a second. Then I realized I should have ordered more because this is absolutely going to be my new go-to dinner party host gift. If fancy smells aren’t your thing for whatever reason (allergies, sensitivities, or disliking nonfood scents in the kitchen), you’ll be happy to know that Naomi also offers a fragrance-free option alongside two scented soaps. It offers the same luxe feel as their scented soap, but instead of volcanic rock, it exfoliates with tiny bits of biodegradable jojoba wax. And if you love the scent as much as I do, Naomi also makes a scrub-free hand soap that smells just as lovely. My bathroom sink is next.

item.title: REVIEW: Why This It-Girl Ski Brand Is My Go-To Every Single Winter
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler
If there’s one thing I take almost as seriously as chasing some good snow, it’s having the right wardrobe to go with it. I’m a lifelong snowboarder, a fairly recent convert to skiing, and someone who has spent plenty of winters bouncing between mountains on the east coast and out west. I’ve learned that the best of the best ski gear needs to do a lot more than look good in a lodge photo. It has to hold up through long lift rides, changing conditions, unexpected snowfall, and the occasional unglamorous tumble. But that doesn’t mean style needs to take a backseat. In fact, I’d argue that the two should go hand in hand. That's a big part of why the popular ski brand, Halfdays, first caught my attention three years ago—and why I keep coming back season after season. Founded in 2020 by former Olympic freestyle aerial skier Kiley McKinnon and Ariana Ferweda, Halfdays came onto the ski scene with a refreshing take: women's ski apparel that actually considers women. Not just smaller versions of men’s gear or the usual boxy, so-called unisex silhouettes, but (finally) thoughtfully designed outerwear that takes fit, function, and fashion all very seriously. The outdoor apparel industry has come a long way, but finding technical pieces that feel just as considered aesthetically as they are functional on the mountain can still be a bit of a treasure hunt. So as someone who has accumulated her fair share of ski and snowboard gear over the years, I immediately fell in love with the brand’s mission, and eventually, the gear itself. While I’ve come to adore its ski suits, bibs, and winter jackets, Halfdays' assortment has expanded beyond the big-ticket ski uniform. The brand offers sweat-wicking baselayers, cozy fleeces, everyday outdoor staples, and chic accessories that make sense well beyond your stay at a ski resort. My favorite pieces from Halfdays keep me feeling comfortable and put together on harsh winter days in New York City too, from knit headbands that cover my ears to winter leggings and warm socks that aren’t too thick. Of course, Halfdays isn’t the same brand it was when I first discovered it. What began as a ski-focused label has evolved into an outdoor brand with spring and summer collections spanning hiking, running, and more warm-weather pursuits. Its arrival at major retailers like Nordstrom, REI, and Backcountry, the opening of its Denver flagship (along with plenty of other storefronts), and a string of collaborations have helped solidify it as a functional brand for every outdoor adventurer. That said, the brand has been having some fun with its fashion credentials, most recently teaming up with Gigi Hadid’s Guest in Residence on an eight-piece winter capsule. The result is a nostalgic take on mountainwear, bringing Guest in Residence’s signature knitwear looks to Halfdays' mountain-ready vibes, with playful retro details that feel just as at home at après-ski as they do on the slopes. On the performance side, though, I’m excited about the brand’s newest launch: Halfdays has officially joined forces with Gore-Tex for its most technical outerwear collection yet. From down jackets and shells to bibs and mittens, the colorful collection brings together trusted waterproof, windproof, and breathable technology with the fit and design that initially made me fall for Halfdays in the first place. As another winter of snow chasing commences, I’m giving my cold-weather wardrobe yet another Halfdays refresh. Below, my tried-and-true ski season favorites from Halfdays, along with a few winter staples I’ve got my eye on.
